nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the Black American novel and the protest
literary_identity: Novelist and memoirist; the author of Native Son and Black Boy, the central Black American writer of the 1940s.
biography: Born Richard Nathaniel Wright on the Rucker plantation near Roxie, Mississippi, on 4 September 1908; he grew up in poverty in Mississippi, Memphis and Chicago, joined the Communist Party, and published Uncle Tom's Children (1938), Native Son (1940) and Black Boy (1945). He moved to Paris in 1946 and died there on 28 November 1960.
literary_profile: Richard Wright was the central Black American writer of the 1940s: Native Son created the modern Black American novel and Black Boy one of the great American memoirs, and his work made the reality of American racial violence visible to the world and opened the way for the civil rights literature of the next generation.
stylistic_characteristics: The naturalist accumulation of detail; the protest and the documentary; the bigger Thomas and the courtroom; the first-person memoir of hunger and violence; the plain, hard, urgent prose.
intellectual_concerns: Race, the colour line, and the New Negro; the Depression, unemployment, and the hunger march; the American city, the machine, and the moneyed metropolis; slavery, emancipation, and the unfinished Reconstruction.
historical_significance: Richard Wright was the central Black American writer of the 1940s: Native Son created the modern Black American novel and Black Boy one of the great American memoirs, and his work made the reality of American racial violence visible to the world.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; the muckraking novel and the socialist expose
literary_identity: Novelist and socialist; the author of The Jungle, the most influential American protest novel ever written.
biography: Born Upton Beall Sinclair Jr in Baltimore on 20 September 1878; he wrote pulp fiction to pay for his education, joined the Socialist Party, and published The Jungle in 1906. King Coal (1917), Oil! (1927), Boston (1928) and the eleven Lanny Budd novels followed, and he won the Pulitzer Prize in 1943. He died in Bound Brook, New Jersey, on 25 November 1968.
literary_profile: Upton Sinclair wrote The Jungle, the most influential American protest novel ever written: it led directly to the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act of 1906, and it founded the American muckraking novel and the literature of industrial horror.
stylistic_characteristics: The documentary accumulation of the stockyards; the immigrant family and the wage slavery; the naturalist detail of filth and corruption; the socialist argument carried by narrative; the plain, urgent, journalistic prose.
intellectual_concerns: Wage labour, the strike, and the two nations; industrial wealth, accumulation, and the gospel of accumulation; the American city, the machine, and the moneyed metropolis; democracy, individualism, and the American experiment.
historical_significance: Upton Sinclair wrote The Jungle, the most influential American protest novel ever written: it led directly to the Pure Food and Drug Act and the Meat Inspection Act of 1906, and it founded the American muckraking novel and the literature of industrial horror.

literary_identity: Novelist, poet and journalist; the author of Nightwood, one of the great modernist novels in English.
biography: Born Djuna Chappell Barnes at Cornwall-on-Hudson, New York, on 12 June 1892; she worked as a journalist in New York, published A Book (1923), Ryder (1928) and Ladies Almanack (1928), and moved to Paris in 1921, where Nightwood was written and published in 1936 with an introduction by T. S. Eliot. She returned to New York and lived as a recluse until her death on 18 June 1982.
literary_profile: Djuna Barnes wrote Nightwood, one of the great modernist novels in English and the finest novel of the expatriate lesbian Paris: its prose, its portrait of Robin Vote and its exploration of sexual obsession made it a central text of modernism, admired by Eliot, Joyce and the whole expatriate avant-garde.
stylistic_characteristics: The baroque, incantatory prose; the monologue of the doctor and the priest; the nocturnal Paris of the expatriates; the refusal of plot in favour of the scene; the obsessive repetition of the image.
intellectual_concerns: Sexuality, the new psychology; exile, expatriation, and the lost generation; the absurd, the void; art versus life, and the romance of the artist.
historical_significance: Djuna Barnes wrote Nightwood, one of the great modernist novels in English and the finest novel of the expatriate lesbian Paris: its prose, its portrait of Robin Vote and its exploration of sexual obsession made it a central text of modernism.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Anglo-Irish; the novel of consciousness and the Big House
literary_identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the finest Anglo-Irish novelist of the century and one of the great English novelists of the modern period.
biography: Born Elizabeth Dorothea Cole Bowen at 15 Herbert Place, Dublin, on 7 June 1899; she grew up at Bowen's Court in County Cork and in England, and published Encounters (1923), The Last September (1929), The House in Paris (1935) and The Death of the Heart (1938). She worked as an air-raid warden in London in the war, and The Heat of the Day (1948) followed. She died in London on 22 February 1973.
literary_profile: Elizabeth Bowen was the finest Anglo-Irish novelist of the century: The Last September gave the Irish troubles their great novel of the Big House, The Death of the Heart is one of the finest English novels of the period, and her short stories made her the master of the modern story of consciousness.
stylistic_characteristics: The image that carries the emotion; the dialogue that circles and evades; the child's eye and the adult's failure; the Big House and the empty room; the precise, sensuous, exact prose.
intellectual_concerns: Ireland, Home Rule, and the national question; the First World War and the myth of sacrifice; sexuality, the new psychology; exile, expatriation, and the lost generation.
historical_significance: Elizabeth Bowen was the finest Anglo-Irish novelist of the century: The Last September gave the Irish troubles their great novel of the Big House, The Death of the Heart is one of the finest English novels of the period, and her stories made her the master of the modern story of consciousness.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Dominican-British; the woman alone and the colonial return
literary_identity: Novelist and short-story writer; the author of Wide Sargasso Sea and the great novelist of the woman alone in Paris and London.
biography: Born Ella Gwendolen Rees Williams in Roseau, Dominica, on 24 August 1890; she came to England at sixteen, worked as a chorus girl and a mannequin, and published The Left Bank (1927), Quartet (1928), After Leaving Mr Mackenzie (1931), Voyage in the Dark (1934) and Good Morning, Midnight (1939). She disappeared from view and returned in 1966 with Wide Sargasso Sea. She died at Exeter on 14 May 1979.
literary_profile: Jean Rhys was the great novelist of the woman alone in Paris and London: her five early novels made the modern novel of the exploited woman, and Wide Sargasso Sea gave the colonial woman and the mad wife of Jane Eyre their own voice, becoming one of the central English novels of the century.
stylistic_characteristics: The first-person narrative of the woman without money; the short, flat, repetitive sentence; the hotel room and the bar; the sudden memory of the Caribbean; the refusal of self-pity and of consolation.
intellectual_concerns: Sexuality, the new psychology; exile, expatriation, and the lost generation; the woman question, married disability, and the New Woman; empire, the imperial idea, and its discontents.
historical_significance: Jean Rhys was the great novelist of the woman alone in Paris and London: her early novels made the modern novel of the exploited woman, and Wide Sargasso Sea gave the colonial woman and the mad wife of Jane Eyre their own voice, becoming one of the central English novels of the century.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the parody of the rural novel
literary_identity: Novelist, poet and journalist; the author of Cold Comfort Farm, the funniest English novel of the 1930s.
biography: Born Stella Dorothea Gibbons in Kentish Town, London, on 5 January 1902; she worked as a journalist for the Evening Standard and the Lady, and published Cold Comfort Farm in 1932, winning the Femina Vie Heureuse Prize. She went on to write some twenty-five novels, including Nightingale Wood (1938) and Westwood (1946), and died in London on 19 December 1989.
literary_profile: Stella Gibbons wrote Cold Comfort Farm, the funniest English novel of the 1930s and the perfect parody of the rural novel: its heroine Flora Poste and her campaign of common sense against the gloom of the farm made it a permanent classic and the definitive satire of the Hardy-Lawrence tradition.
stylistic_characteristics: The parody of the rural novel and its dialect; the comic catalogue of the gloomy farm; the sensible heroine against the romantic tradition; the footnote and the pastiche; the light, dry, exact prose.
intellectual_concerns: The countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy; the woman question, married disability, and the New Woman; the absurd, the void.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: British; the regional novel and the feminist journalism
literary_identity: Novelist, journalist and feminist; the author of South Riding, the great English regional novel of the 1930s.
biography: Born Winifred Holtby at Rudston, Yorkshire, on 23 June 1898; she served in the Women's Army Auxiliary Corps in the First World War, read at Somerville College, Oxford, and became the closest friend of Vera Brittain. Anderby Wold (1923), The Crowded Street (1924), Mandoa, Mandoa! (1933) and South Riding (1936, posthumous) followed, with her feminist journalism. She died in London on 29 September 1935.
literary_profile: Winifred Holtby wrote South Riding, the great English regional novel of the 1930s and one of the finest English feminist novels of the century: her portrait of a Yorkshire county council and its women made the local administration into epic, and her journalism made her the central feminist voice of the decade.
stylistic_characteristics: The documentary detail of the county council; the multiple plot of a whole community; the feminist heroine and her public work; the plain, vigorous, unsentimental prose; the Yorkshire landscape and its people.
intellectual_concerns: The Depression, unemployment, and the hunger march; the woman question, married disability, and the New Woman; regional identity and the American sectional character; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy.

literary_identity: Novelist and journalist; the author of The Diary of a Provincial Lady, the funniest English comic diary of the century.
biography: Born Edmee Elizabeth Monica de la Pasture at Steyning, Sussex, on 9 June 1890; she worked as a nurse in the First World War and as a VAD, and published Zella Sees Herself (1917), Consequences (1919), The Diary of a Provincial Lady (1930) and its sequels, and some thirty novels. She died in Cullompton, Devon, on 2 December 1943.
literary_profile: E. M. Delafield wrote The Diary of a Provincial Lady, the funniest English comic diary of the century and one of the great English comic works: its self-deprecating narrator, her household and her social embarrassments made it a permanent classic, and Consequences is one of the finest feminist novels of the period.
stylistic_characteristics: The comic diary with its deadpan self-mockery; the household detail of the provincial middle class; the elliptical and the understated; the running cast of Lady Boxe and Mademoiselle; the light, exact, self-aware prose.
intellectual_concerns: The suburb, the villa, and the new domesticity; the woman question, married disability, and the New Woman; class, the servant problem, and the new democracy; the countryside, the vanishing rural world, and the motor road.
